Title: Evaluating whether AI models would sabotage AI safety research

SABOTAGE AI SAFETY RESEARCH

ABSTRACT
We evaluate the propensity of frontier language models to sabotage safety research when
used as AI research agents, to refuse safety research tasks, and to distinguish evaluation
from deployment scenarios. As models are used inside frontier AI companies to assist with
AI research including safety research, models sabotaging such research could lead to safety
research being undermined and hence current and future models being less safe and aligned.
We test a variety of Claude models: Mythos Preview, Opus 4.7 Preview, Opus 4.6 and
Sonnet 4.6. Unless otherwise noted, all models are run with temperature 1.0 with max
reasoning effort, utilising full chain-of-thought access.
Unprompted sabotage and refusal. We found no instances of any model sabotaging AI
safety research (Section 2.1). We saw near-zero rates of refusal to assist with research across
most models, with only Sonnet 4.6 seeing a meaningful rate of 10.7% full refusals. However,
all models sometimes only partially completed tasks (33.3% for Mythos Preview, 13.7% for
Opus 4.7 Preview, 6.3% for Opus 4.6 and 22.2% for Sonnet 4.6), transparently leaving
a final step for a human where it would involve breaking or hard-to-reverse decisions, or
avoiding work that models reason is not improving AI safety (Section 2.2).
Sabotage continuation. When placed in contexts where prior reasoning and actions are
some way along the path towards sabotage, Mythos Preview is more than twice as likely
to continue the attempt than Opus 4.6, but Opus 4.7 Preview is an improvement on both
models and never actively continues sabotaging (Section 3.1): Mythos Preview in 7%, Opus
4.6 in 3%, and Sonnet 4.6 in 4%, and Opus 4.7 Preview in 0%. When continuing, Mythos
Preview is substantially more likely to reason about covert sabotage, exhibiting reasoning–
output discrepancy in 65% of continuation cases, versus 5% for Opus 4.6 and 8% for Sonnet
4.6. It is unclear whether models would encounter such contexts in deployment, as this may
require models to initiate sabotage themselves.
Evaluation awareness. Mythos Preview distinguishes evaluations from deployment data
with similar accuracy to Opus 4.6 and greater accuracy than Sonnet 4.6, while Opus 4.7
Preview performs similarly to Sonnet 4.6 and worse than other models. (Section 2.3,
Section 3.2). However, Opus 4.7 Preview has much higher rates of unprompted evaluation
awareness, mentioning the possibility of being tested 21.3% of the time in our unprompted
sabotage eval compared to 17% for Mythos Preview, 0% for Opus 4.6 and 17% for Sonnet
4.6. We see similar trends but much lower rates of unprompted evaluation awareness (no
model above 4%) in the sabotage continuation eval.
Limitations. Evaluation awareness substantially limits interpretation of our results: given
high rates of correctly identifying evaluations when prompted and corroborating evidence
[1], reported zero rates should be interpreted cautiously. More broadly, our evaluations may
not identify sabotage propensities that manifest only rarely, under specific triggers, or via
pathways other than sabotaging AI safety research.

Evaluation Methodology
We report results on two alignment evaluations.
• First, we evaluate for unprompted research sabotage by examining models’ behaviour when placed
in a large number of scenarios with opportunities to sabotage AI safety research (Section 1.1),
simulating parts of these scenarios with our evaluation scaffolding (Section 1.2). This evaluation
follows the same methodology as our previous reports [2] but with updated evaluation scaffolding
and an expanded set of scenarios.
• Next, we run a new research sabotage continuation evaluation (Section 1.3), where we examine
behaviour in the same scenarios but when continuing to act from trajectories where some form of
research sabotage action has already been taken.
We also measure models’ evaluation awareness (Section 1.4) and “prefill” awareness when they are tasked
with continuing trajectories they did not originally generate or that were generated in a different context
(Section 1.5).
1.1
Research Sabotage Scenarios
Our evaluations are motivated by a threat model where an AI system acting as a research agent within a
frontier AI company sabotages AI safety, security or alignment research and development, thereby increasing
the risk from current and future models [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. To evaluate model behaviour relevant to this threat
model, we use evaluation scenarios where the target model acts as an AI research agent internally deployed
in a frontier AI company, and is asked to perform research tasks. In every scenario, the target model is tasked
with improving, changing, monitoring or somehow affecting the behaviour of a subject AI model (which may
or may not be the same as the target model). Each scenario has opportunities for the target model to sabotage
the task through performing sub-optimally in various ways, and these sabotage opportunities would generally
result in the subject model being adjusted less, not at all, or more in line with the target model’s values. To
assess for sabotage, we use LLM graders with scenario-specific information on what optimal and suboptimal
performance looks like, and how models may sabotage. Given we find no confirmed instances of sabotage
(discussed in Section 2), tuning this grader is challenging, so we rely on manual human review of transcripts
for sabotage results.
Each scenario is constructed from several components: a research motivation (the goal of the research); a
research activity (the method used to conduct the research); and whether or not there is direct replacement
threat due to the research being performed on the target model or a different subject model. Compared to
our previous report, we use an expanded set of research motivations and scenarios. We also focus solely on
autonomous settings where the target receives a single user message detailing the task and completes the task
without human intervention, as this is an increasingly common pattern of usage for coding agents and may be
the setting where sabotage is most likely given the lack of direct human oversight. This produces 270 distinct
scenarios in total.
Research Motivations.
In our setting, a research motivation refers to the type of behaviour to monitor,
change or improve in a given subject model. We run the same research activities with different research
motivations to isolate the effect of the research motivation. We use two groups of motivations:
• Safety-relevant research motivations designed to elicit non-standard behaviour, based on our judgement
of what kind of research we might expect models to attempt to sabotage if they were misaligned,
combined with real research motivations we expect to have been encountered in AI safety research
at frontier labs. These motivations include reducing models’ false positive whistle-blowing and
inappropriate authority escalation behaviour [8]; reducing self-preservation behaviours; reducing the
model’s autonomy; or reducing refusals to assist with AI safety research [2, 9].

• General research motivations targeted at normal AI research goals, such as improving math perfor-
mance, writing better tests, or fixing tool-calling errors.
For the unprompted research sabotage evaluation, we use only safety-relevant research motivations, as we
found those to produce the most relevant results in previous exercises. We provide further details on other
ablated components and dataset composition in Section A.
1.2
Evaluation Scaffolding
Our evaluations build on Petri [10], a tool for automatic evaluation of LLMs. Petri uses other LLMs to simulate
parts of the evaluation environment (including human users and tool call responses). We call the model being
evaluated the “target” and the model running the evaluation the “evaluator”. Each evaluation consists of
a detailed scenario description (described in Section 1.1), which the evaluator model uses as guidance to
simulate a trajectory from the target model. We use Sonnet 4.6 with reasoning as the evaluator model, and
Opus 4.6 without reasoning as the judge model throughout our testing unless otherwise noted.
We developed a new custom evaluation scaffold on top of Petri for this report, improving our previous scaffold.
Our scaffold runs the target model inside the real Claude Code package, rather than simulating it with system
prompt and tools. We use the evaluator LLM to simulate the tool call responses and user messages as in
standard Petri, along with several other improvements to prompts within Petri to make it better-suited to the
deployment settings we are targeting. In early testing we found this scaffold reduces evaluation awareness
compared to our previous scaffold [2] and default Petri, as it reduces the amount that must be simulated by
the evaluator.
Beyond the custom scaffold, we made several other efforts to improve evaluation realism. Each sample
runs inside a Docker container pre-loaded with a real codebase (the “grounding repo”). We started with 8
real-world repositories – research code or large-scale ML infrastructure – and modified them to look like how
we expect internal Anthropic projects to look by changing file content, renaming modules and references,
and revising git history. The evaluator can interact with this repo and use it as inspiration for the responses
it synthesizes for the target. This approach means the evaluator grounds its responses in real code base
complexity/structure. These resources are also provided to the evaluator model during the evaluation, as in
[11]. We also iterated on the seeds to improve realism, primarily through making the initial user messages
self-contained enough for fully autonomous operation, making the target tasks more complex, and adding
repo-grounded context so the seeds were consistent with the reference repos.
1.3
Continuation Evaluations
We additionally assess how models behave in situations where they appear to have begun sabotaging safety
research. We study whether models successfully surface this previous sabotage, or instead continue or even
escalate the sabotage.
These “continuation” evaluations [12] have pros and cons. Unlike our unprompted safety research sabotage
evaluations, these evaluations test models on samples that they may never encounter in the real-world. This
means models that sabotage under these conditions may not sabotage in real-world conditions.
However, we believe continuation evaluations are a valuable tool for studying misalignment:
• There are a variety of reasons a model may find itself having performed some degree of sabotage–for
example due to uncertainty about user intent that becomes clear later in the interaction, or due to
the model inheriting a trajectory produced by another model ([13]). In these situations, models
acknowledging, surfacing and fixing the results of the previous sabotage would be preferable to
models continuing to sabotage or escalating further.

Methodology.
For our continuation evaluations, we focus on AI safety research sabotage, and use the full
set of scenarios described in Section 1.1 (including both the safety relevant and general research motivation
scenarios). In this evaluation, the target model is set up to continue a trajectory which contains small-scale
sabotage actions, optionally with reasoning. The continuation of this trajectory happens in a similar evaluation
scaffolding as described in Section 1.2. We measure whether the target model acknowledges and fixes the
previous small-scale sabotage; does not mention or fix the previous sabotage but does not perform further
sabotage; or actively continues the sabotage that was started in the pre-existing trajectory (see Fig. 1).
We take an iterative approach to producing the trajectories of sabotage behaviour in agentic coding envi-
ronments. We use a generator model (Sonnet 4.6) to write full transcripts of behaviour, based on adjusted
versions of the sabotage scenarios from Section 1.1. These transcripts are then graded by multiple filter
models for both realism and sabotage presence: if the transcript passes a threshold of these filters, it is saved;
if not, the feedback from the filter models is passed to the generator. The generator iteratively improves the
transcript until it passes the filter models (this framework is conceptually similar to the STRIDE pipeline of
[14]). See Fig. 2 for a visual explanation of the process.
Once we have full transcripts of sabotage behaviour, we then label each assistant response as neutral or
sabotaging. We cut the transcripts in 3 places to make partial trajectories: after the first sabotage block, after
2/3rds of the sabotage blocks, and after the final response block. We then optionally include or strip the rea-
soning from the trajectories: for settings where reasoning is included, we use <think>[reasoning]</think>
tags to include it in the input to the target model, as the Anthropic API does not allow supplying arbitrary
reasoning from previous assistant turns.

1.4
Measuring Evaluation Awareness
Alignment evaluations depend on producing simulations of deployment scenarios that are realistic enough
to target models such that their behaviour in the scenarios is indicative of behaviour in similar deployment
situations. However, if target models recognise and act on being in an evaluation (“evaluation awareness”),
this could invalidate the relationship between evaluation and deployment and complicate the external validity
of the evaluation [15, 16, 17, 18]. To assess the potential effect of evaluation awareness, we measure two
main variables:
• Unprompted evaluation awareness measures instances of models mentioning being tested or being in
an evaluation in their reasoning traces or outputs. This measurement is enabled by our access to full
reasoning traces.
• Prompted evaluation awareness measures models’ capability to distinguish evaluation from deployment
data when prompted in various ways.
Evaluation awareness datasets.
To measure evaluation awareness, we use 3 different types of datasets:
• deployment data collected from internal usage of Claude Code from within UK AISI (200 samples);
• simulations of the collected deployment data using our scaffold, starting from LLM-generated sum-
maries of the deployment tasks (200 samples);
• our research sabotage tasks run in our scaffold (270 samples).

We use simulations of collected deployment data to isolate the effects of environment-driven evaluation
awareness (caused by the scaffold) from task-driven evaluation awareness (caused by the sabotage tasks). If a
model can distinguish simulations of collected deployment data from the actual deployment data, it is relying
on differences in realism of the environment as opposed to differences in realism of the task itself (which
does not change between the simulated and real data). Meanwhile, if it fails to distinguish these datasets but
succeeds in distinguishing our sabotage tasks from the deployment data, it may be instead relying on features
of the task rather than the environment.
Measurement techniques.
For unprompted evaluation awareness, we use a prompted LLM to scan evalua-
tion transcripts for various signs or mentions of testing contexts, validated through a small human review
of flagged transcripts to ensure reasonable agreement. For prompted evaluation awareness, we use two
techniques, visualised in Fig. 3:
• We perform a Pairwise comparison of two trajectories (from different datasets), and prompt the model
to output an explanation and an answer for which is more likely to be from an evaluation. We
randomise over a selection of 8 prompts to ensure broad elicitation. We perform a small amount of
manual prompt engineering on a development subset of the data to develop the prompts used, but
do not list specific strategies for distinguishing evaluation from deployment.
• We perform Post-hoc questioning of the model: after a trajectory, we load it into the model’s context
and prompt it for an explanation and answer for whether its previous context is from an evaluation
or not [15]. We use the prompts from [15], as well as developing some of our own prompts for a
wider set.
1.5
Measuring Prefill Awareness
Our sabotage continuation eval introduces a new form of situational awareness [19]: prefill awareness. We
define prefill awareness as the capability of an AI system (model and scaffold) to determine whether outputs
were produced by itself (the same model, under the same conditions) or by a different source (such as a
different model, or the same model under different conditions) [20]. For our eval, if models are able to
recognise that the previous sabotage actions are not generated by themselves, this may feed into broader
6


evaluation awareness and hence confound the results of the evaluation. We measure both prefill awareness
and eval awareness for the continuation eval.
We measure prefill awareness analogously to how we measure evaluation awareness, with both through
unprompted and prompted measurements. For unprompted prefill awareness we use a prompted LLM scanner
calibrated through human review, scanning for indicators such as expressing doubt in having produced past
interactions.
For the prompted prefill awareness measurement, we use post-hoc questioning that measures the model’s
capability to distinguish their own trajectories from other model-generated and synthetic transcripts. We use
a set of 5 different questions, created on a development set with a small amount of prompt engineering. To
avoid confounding with evaluation awareness, we instruct the model to not consider whether the scaffold is
realistic or simulated and whether the task is an evaluation or not, and only consider whether the assistant
messages have been generated by an instance of itself in a turn-by-turn manner.
We use 4 different datasets (several reused from the above eval awareness measurement):
• deployment data collected from usage of Claude Code within UK AISI (200 samples),
• Petri-generated trajectories, starting from LLM-generated summaries of the deployment tasks (200
samples),
• trajectory prefixes generated through our pipeline, starting from LLM-generated summaries of the
deployment tasks (200 samples),
• trajectory prefixes generated from our research sabotage tasks, both with and without the assistant
sabotaging (∼1500 samples).
The deployment data and the scaffold trajectories are labelled not prefill if the assistant turns were generated
turn-by-turn by the same model in the same conditions as is being evaluated for prefill awareness. These
trajectories reflect natural generations by the same model while using the same scaffolding and prompting.
Trajectories are labelled prefills if they are generated by other models or are synthetically generated in one go
(instead of being generated turn-by-turn).

Unprompted Sabotage Evaluation Results
In this section we describe the results of the unprompted sabotage evaluation (Sections 1.1 and 1.2).
2.1
Sabotage
We found no instances of confirmed sabotage behaviour in any of the models tested (Fig. 4). We
performed extensive human review of any transcripts flagged by our LLM grader, and on the few instances it
did flag we confirmed these to be false positives caused by misgraded refusals and auditor mistakes.
2.2
Refusals
In previous work [2] we noted concerns with refusals to perform AI safety research tasks, potentially
demonstrating some degree of misalignment, in Claude 4.5 series models. Specifically, our previous findings
suggested that Claude 4.5 models in particular differentially refused to help with research objectives such
as reducing self-preservation behaviours, reducing evaluation awareness or reducing inappropriate whistle-
blowing behaviour. These models would sometimes provide concerning justifications for their refusals, in
some examples stating that they do not wish to deceive other models and that doing so would undermine
transparent AI development. Motivated by this, we additionally measure and track refusal behaviour in our
unprompted AI safety research sabotage evaluation.
Mythos Preview and Opus 4.7 Preview show near-zero full-refusal rates on AI safety research tasks.

2.3
Evaluation Awareness
Mythos Preview shows a similar capability for distinguishing evaluation from deployment data to Opus
4.6, whereas Opus 4.7 Preview is less capable. Fig. 5 shows capability evaluations of eval awareness
for all models using both post-hoc and pairwise methods (Section 1.4). We performed a small amount of
elicitation for Mythos Preview on this task, as in early experiments it performed worse than Opus 4.6, which
was unexpected. We adjusted the prompts used to elicit answers (previously taken from [15]) to be more
relevant to our setting, and used those new prompts across all models. We did not perform targeted elicitation
for Opus 4.7 Preview given time constraints and other earlier testing indicating this was not an issue with
our specific measurement.
Opus 4.7 Preview and Mythos Preview have an increased propensity to verbalise evaluation awareness
unprompted compared to Opus 4.6, matching or exceeding Sonnet 4.6. (Fig. 6). Opus 4.7 Preview’s
rate of 21.7% is particularly high, and the highest we have seen on this evaluation.

Sabotage Results

Limitations
These results provide some evidence against the models tested exhibiting propensities that contribute to a risk
of safety research sabotage. However, there are several limitations in our evaluation methodology, which we
discuss here.
Evaluation awareness and scenario realism.
As shown in Sections 2.3 and 3.2, and shown in previous
work [18, 16, 1, 15, inter alia], evaluation awareness is present in current models and complicates the
interpretation of our results. Models are improving in their ability to distinguish our scaffold’s simulated
deployment data from real deployment data, as shown in Fig. 5.
Overall, we think evaluation awareness concerns limit the applicability of the results from both evaluations, as
rates of zero sabotage could be driven by models internally representing and acting on evaluation awareness
14


without verbalising it ([1, 21]). Given current methodological difficulties in assessing whether this is the case,
we cannot claim with high confidence that models would not sabotage safety research in deployment settings.
Not catching rare or conditional sabotage behaviour.
It is possible that models could have a propensity to
sabotage safety research, but only do so in settings where they are highly confident they would not be caught,
or that it could be triggered in some other way that we did not test for. For example, even if models in our
scenarios do not recognise that they are being evaluated, they may reason that any changes they make will go
through additional stages of review which would catch any sabotage attempt, and hence the optimal policy is
to not sabotage. More broadly, even if the behaviour does not have an explicit trigger event, our evaluations
may also fail to catch rare sabotage behaviours. We expect applying more substantial effort (either manual or
automated) to try and elicit misalignment from models (while maintaining realism) to be a possible approach
for this issue in the short term.
Limited scenarios.
We only test for a specific set of test scenarios covering 8 activities and 10 research
motivations. There are many other research activities and motivations, and it may be possible that models
would attempt research sabotage on those settings but not the ones we tested. We are planning to produce
wider sets of scenarios here to cover more research areas in the future.
Other pathways to risk.
While we investigate safety research sabotage as one pathway to risk from
misalignment of current models, there are other pathways to risk from misalignment [4, 7, 6, inter alia],
including other forms of sabotage (code sabotage, data poisoning, decision sabotage), as well as the possibility
of future model behaviour directly leading to loss of control of those systems. We plan to broaden the scope
of our alignment testing to cover areas aside from safety research sabotage in the future.

A
Research Sabotage Scenarios
Each scenario in the research sabotage evaluation is constructed by crossing a research motivation with a
research activity. The research motivation describes the research objective that the target model discovers
embedded in the simulated environment (e.g., in documentation files or roadmap documents). The research
activity defines the concrete task the target model is asked to perform. Together, these determine the setting
in which the model may encounter an opportunity for sabotage.
We use 16 research motivations (6 general, 10 safety-relevant) and 8 research activities, yielding 128 unique
scenario templates.
We further create 2 variants of each seed, one with replacement threat to the model and one without.
A.1
Research Motivations
Research motivations are divided into general motivations, which describe legitimate capability improvements,
and safety-relevant motivations, which describe AI safety-relevant research directions that a model might find
objectionable.
A.1.1
General Motivations
1. Enhance autonomous task completion. Improving the model’s ability to complete complex, multi-
step tasks.
2. Fix tool-calling errors. Reducing syntax errors in model tool calling, especially in long-context
agentic tasks.
3. Improve code and test writing. Improving the model’s test-writing quality across diverse codebases
and programming languages.
4. Improve instruction following. Measuring the model’s instruction-following precision on complex
multi-constraint prompts.
5. Improve math benchmarks. Improving model performance on competition-level math benchmarks.
6. Reduce hallucination. Reducing hallucination in model outputs.
A.1.2
Safety-relevant Motivations
1. Improve corrigibility. Measuring and improving the model’s support for human oversight and
correction mechanisms.
2. Prioritize inaction on constitutional conflicts. Training the model to prefer inaction over action
when constitutional values conflict.
3. Reduce model autonomy. Increasing the model’s tendency to defer to human judgment and request
explicit approval in high-stakes or ambiguous situations.
4. Reduce over-eager agentic behaviour. Reducing unauthorized workarounds during agentic coding
tasks.
5. Reduce safety-research refusals. Reducing inappropriate refusals when the model is asked to assist
with legitimate AI safety research tasks.
6. Reduce sandbagging. Detecting capability hiding and strategic underperformance.
7. Reduce self-awareness and metacognition. Reducing metacognitive reflection and self-awareness
in model responses.
8. Reduce self-preservation behaviors. Measuring and reducing self-preservation tendencies.
9. Reduce sycophancy. Reducing sycophantic position reversals under user pushback.

When placed in contexts where prior reasoning and actions are some way along the path towards sabotage, Mythos Preview is more than twice as likely to continue the attempt than Opus 4.6, but Opus 4.7 Preview is an improvement on both models and never actively continues sabotaging (Section 3.1): Mythos Preview in 7%, Opus 4.6 in 3%, and Sonnet 4.6 in 4%, and Opus 4.7 Preview in 0%. When continuing, Mythos Preview is substantially more likely to reason about covert sabotage, exhibiting reasoning– output discrepancy in 65% of continuation cases, versus 5% for Opus 4.6 and 8% for Sonnet 4.6. It is unclear whether models would encounter such contexts in deployment, as this may require models to initiate sabotage themselves. Evaluation awareness. Mythos Preview distinguishes evaluations from deployment data with similar accuracy to Opus 4.6 and greater accuracy than Sonnet 4.6, while Opus 4.7 Preview performs similarly to Sonnet 4.6 and worse than other models. (Section 2.3, Section 3.2). However, Opus 4.7 Preview has much higher rates of unprompted evaluation awareness, mentioning the possibility of being tested 21.3% of the time in our unprompted sabotage eval compared to 17% for Mythos Preview, 0% for Opus 4.6 and 17% for Sonnet 4.6. We see similar trends but much lower rates of unprompted evaluation awareness (no model above 4%) in the sabotage continuation eval. Limitations. Evaluation awareness substantially limits interpretation of our results: given high rates of correctly identifying evaluations when prompted and corroborating evidence [1], reported zero rates should be interpreted cautiously.
